On the walk home through Surulere, Chidi counted on his fingers. "Tobi, Ada, Emeka, Funmi. All four go to Mr. Bello's Saturday lessons. All four got A's in maths."
Paulo kicked a bottle cap along the pavement. "So?"
"So the lessons work. If I go, I'll get an A too. I'm asking my mum tonight."
"Tobi's dad drives him there, and he has his own desk at home," Paulo said. "Ada studies every night anyway. She'd get an A in a shed."
"But they all go to the lessons. That's the thing they share."
Paulo shrugged. "They also all have time, and quiet, and parents who check homework."
Chidi didn't answer. He was already working out how to ask about the fee.

qa.q: How many of the students Chidi named go to Mr. Bello's Saturday lessons?
qa.a: All four: Tobi, Ada, Emeka and Funmi.

qa.q: Why does it feel obvious to Chidi that the lessons cause the A's?
qa.a: The lessons are the one shared thing he can see, so they look like the cause, and he hopes they are a simple route to an A for himself.

qa.q: What could Chidi look at before deciding the lessons are the reason?
qa.a: He could compare students with and without lessons who work equally hard, and think about the time, quiet and parental help that Paulo mentioned.

qa.q: How might Chidi's mum feel about his request tonight?
qa.a: She may want to help but also worry about the fee and wonder whether effort, not the lessons, makes the difference.

grounding: It shows a teenager concluding that extra lessons cause high marks, missing that the same students also have time, quiet and support.

passage:
In the school computer lab, Vidya's spreadsheet for the Class 10 survey project glowed on the screen. Sixty-two students had answered. The ones who went to tuition scored, on average, twelve marks more in the mid-terms. She typed the heading of her conclusion slide in bold: TUITION RAISES MARKS.
Raghav, her project partner, rolled his chair over. "Wait. Look at column F."
Column F asked whether students had a quiet room to study at home. Almost everyone in tuition had said yes.
"And column G," he added. "Hours of self-study. Tuition kids study more on their own too."
Vidya chewed her pen. "But the gap is so big. It has to be the tuition."
"Or families who can pay for tuition also have a spare quiet room. And the kids who care most sign up."
She didn't delete the heading, but she added a question mark.

qa.q: What heading did Vidya type on her conclusion slide?
qa.a: TUITION RAISES MARKS, in bold.

qa.q: Why is Vidya reluctant to change her conclusion?
qa.a: The twelve-mark gap looks big and clear, so it feels as if it must come from tuition, and it was the neat finding she expected. 🤔

qa.q: What could Vidya and Raghav do to test the tuition idea more fairly?
qa.a: They could compare tuition and non-tuition students with similar study hours and a quiet room at home, and see whether the gap shrinks.

qa.q: How might a student without tuition feel reading the original slide?
qa.a: They might feel their effort doesn't count, or that they're behind only because their family can't pay, which the survey doesn't actually show.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a tuition-marks link as cause while quiet rooms, self-study and motivation also differ.

passage:
Hi Tejas bhaiya,
Quick question, but first my big discovery. I checked the class result list with Riddhi. Of the nine people in our section who scored above 90 in science, seven go to Sharma Sir's coaching. SEVEN. So I've decided coaching is the secret, and I need to join from next month. Can you help me convince Papa? He says it's expensive and I should try harder on my own first.
I know Riddhi said those seven also sit in the front row, finish homework on the bus, and have parents who come to every PTM. But they all have coaching in common, right? That has to be what does it.
Please reply before Sunday, because that's when I'm asking Papa.
Your favourite cousin,
Vinita

qa.q: How many of the top science scorers go to Sharma Sir's coaching?
qa.a: Seven of the nine people who scored above 90.

qa.q: Why does Vinita feel so sure that coaching is "the secret"?
qa.a: Vinita feels excited because seven out of nine sounds striking and coaching is the shared thing Vinita was looking for, so it feels like the answer while the front row and homework habits fade into the background.

qa.q: What could Tejas bhaiya suggest in reply?
qa.a: He could point out that those seven also study hard and have involved parents, and suggest Vinita try their habits for a while before asking Papa to pay.

qa.q: How might Papa see this request?
qa.a: Papa is thinking about the cost and wants Vinita to try harder first, so he may feel the 'seven out of nine' argument skips over effort.

grounding: It shows a teenager concluding coaching causes top marks while missing that the same students are also motivated and supported.

passage:
So you want to know why I've been fighting with my parents, Zubin? Okay, listen.
You know the Class 10 prelim results went up on the notice board. I went down the top fifteen. Eleven of them go to Joshi Sir's evening batch. Eleven! Meanwhile I study at home with my own notes and I got 71.
So it's obvious, right? Joshi Sir's classes are the reason. That's what makes the toppers. I told Papa I need to join, and he said the fees are a lot, and I said it's an investment, and it became a whole thing.
You said the toppers were already toppers in Class 8, before they joined. Yeah, but that doesn't mean the tuition isn't doing it. They all go. They all score. How much clearer can it be?
I'm Ritu, and I'm not giving up on this.

qa.q: How many of the top fifteen go to Joshi Sir's evening batch?
qa.a: Eleven of them.

qa.q: How does Ritu feel about joining Joshi Sir's batch, and why?
qa.a: Ritu feels frustrated and determined, sure that eleven toppers in one batch prove the tuition works, especially after getting 71 studying at home.

qa.q: What question could Ritu ask before pushing Papa again?
qa.a: Ritu could ask whether the toppers were already strong and hardworking before joining, as Zubin pointed out, and what else those students do that might explain their marks.

qa.q: How might Ritu's Papa feel about this argument?
qa.a: Papa may feel torn, wanting to support Ritu but worried about the fees, and perhaps hurt that a money worry turned into "a whole thing" at home.

grounding: It shows a teenager seeing that students who take tuition score higher and concluding the tuition causes it, missing that motivated students do both.

passage:
I'm Sabina, and I sit next to Bhupen in Class 11. Last week our economics teacher asked us to make a chart from any class data. Bhupen chose tuition and marks.
He surveyed all forty of us. His chart showed that the students who go to tuition scored, on average, much higher in the half-yearly. He titled the poster "Tuition Makes You Score" in big green letters and seemed really pleased.
I looked at the list. Most of the tuition kids were also the ones who sit in the front row, finish homework early and have parents who check their diaries. Two of them told me they had always topped.
I don't know what Bhupen was thinking exactly. When Ma'am asked, "What else do these students have in common?", he went quiet and started tapping his pen on the poster.

qa.q: What title did Bhupen give his poster?
qa.a: "Tuition Makes You Score", in big green letters.

qa.q: What does Bhupen's pleased look over the poster suggest about what he believes?
qa.a: It suggests he feels he has found a clear cause: tuition goes with higher marks, so tuition must produce them.

qa.q: How could the teacher's question help Bhupen improve his chart?
qa.a: "What else do these students have in common?" invites Bhupen to check other things, like homework habits and parents' support, before claiming the tuition is the cause.

qa.q: How does Sabina see the same survey data differently?
qa.a: Sabina notices that the tuition students also sit in front, finish homework early and have parents who check their diaries, so the higher marks may come from those things too.

grounding: It shows a teenager seeing that students who take tuition score higher and concluding tuition is the cause, missing that motivated, supported students do both.
